turns.text:
I found out from my 9-year-old that my ex has a boyfriend and has already introduced him to our kids. Sunday at 5 I pick them up, and before I've pulled away from the curb Zara says, "Mom has a boyfriend. His name is Nico." Obi adds that he can do a handstand. I didn't even know she was seeing anyone.

We have a signed parenting plan. It says we tell each other before any introduction. She didn't. She had all of Saturday night and Sunday to send me one line. Her defense is that she tried to tell me the week before. What she actually sent was "Can we talk this week? There's something I want to tell you before Zara's party." No hint what it was about. I had a deadline that Friday and asked if it could wait until after the party. She said ok. Then she went ahead anyway.

So yes, I asked the kids some questions on the drive home. I'm their dad. I think she wanted the kids to deliver the news so she wouldn't have to face me. She kept me in the dark and let a 9-year-old do her job. I feel completely blindsided.

What do you make of all this?

Your reaction fits what happened. She agreed to wait, then introduced him anyway, and you found out from Zara in the car. That is a real breach of the plan and a fair reason to feel blindsided.

The text she sent was not notice. "Can we talk, there's something I want to tell you before Zara's party" names a time and withholds the subject. You asked whether it could wait until after the party, and she said ok. That reply is the important part. Once she agreed to wait, going ahead that weekend was a choice, and "I tried the week before" does not cover it. Trying would have been one plain sentence: his name, that she wanted the kids to meet him, and when. She had Saturday night and Sunday to send that after the deadline passed. She did not.

The part I would not treat as fact is that she set the kids up to deliver it so she would not have to face you. That is possible, and conflict avoidance would fit the vague text. It is also possible she had already planned the introduction around the party, decided your "after the party" meant the conversation could slip, and then Zara did what a lot of nine-year-olds do with news this size. "Mom has a boyfriend. His name is Nico" plus a handstand is how a kid reports something novel and exciting. It does not, by itself, prove she coached them. If you hold her to the coached-messenger version and she did not do that, the fight becomes about a motive you cannot prove, and the actual violation gets lost.

Asking who is around your kids is a parent's job. The line that matters is what you do with the answers. Who he is, whether they liked him, whether anything felt off: that is yours to know. How Mom feels about him, what they do when you are not there, anything you would then quote back to her: that puts Zara and Obi in the middle of an adult problem. They already carried the news once. They should not have to carry the argument.

What you can fairly say to her, in writing, is narrow. The plan requires notice before an introduction. Her message did not say she was introducing someone. You asked to talk after the party and she agreed. She introduced him anyway, and you heard it from the kids at pickup. You expect his name and notice before any further introductions, in a message that states the fact, before it happens. Leave the mind-reading out of that message. "You hid this so a nine-year-old would have to tell me" will get you a defense. The timeline will not.

One practical gap: you still do not know much about Nico beyond a name and a handstand. The useful next information is whether this person will be around the kids regularly, not a reconstruction of Saturday night from Zara. Get that from her.

Yes. On the part that matters, you are right.

She owed you notice before an introduction. What she sent was a request to talk, with the subject left out. You asked to wait until after the party, she agreed, and she introduced him anyway. You heard it from Zara at the curb. That is a broken agreement, and feeling blindsided is the normal response to it.

The only piece that is still an inference is why she did it. You can be certain she did not tell you. You cannot yet be certain she meant for a nine-year-old to do it for her.
